sum: SK Hynix just forecast a memory shortage stretching years into the future, and the chip equipment makers who build the factories to fix it are surging. But supply bottlenecks and China exposure could determine whether this rally has real legs.

Chip equipment stocks are leading a third straight day of gains across semiconductors as SK Hynix‘s (NASDAQ:SKHY) view that the memory shortage lasts into 2030 points to years of fab building. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) stock is at $253, up 5% in early trading.
Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) stock is at $412, up 4%. Additionally, KLA (NASDAQ:KLAC) stock is at $158, up 3%.
Why SK Hynix’s 2030 Shortage Call Lifts Chip Equipment Makers

SK Hynix said on October 28 that its quarterly profit rose sevenfold and that it expects a memory supply shortage to last into 2030. The memory maker tied that view to surging AI inference demand and spreading adoption in robotics and autonomous driving.

That outlook carries the most weight for the companies that equip chip factories. Relieving a memory shortage requires more output, and more output requires new clean rooms, wafer fabrication tools and advanced packaging gear, which is what Lam Research, Applied Materials and KLA sell.

Chip stocks have now climbed for three sessions after worries about AI spending and neocloud debt weighed on the sector in recent weeks. Over the past month, Lam Research stock is down 20%, Applied Materials stock is down 15% and KLA stock is down 16%.

sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Shares of KLA (KLAC) lost 12.1% in the month ending October 20, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.6%. KLA has not fallen alone. Two of its closest peers, Applied Materials and Lam Research, fell 12.8% each over the same dates. If the wider market turns too, how far has KLA stock fallen in past market shocks, and how long did it stay down?

During the 2008-2009 financial crisis, KLA stock lost 69% while the S&P 500 lost 53%. That marked the steepest decline for the shares across the 15 market shocks they have traded through since 2007. During the 2022 inflation and Fed tightening shock, KLA fell 39%, compared with 24% for the index. Across all of those shocks, KLA dropped an average of 20.4%, a deeper decline than the 15.8% average for the S&P 500.

The stock typically recovered within a few months. The median recovery time from the stock’s low to its earlier high was 2.3 months. Two recoveries took significantly more time. KLA needed 26.6 months after the financial crisis. Following the summer 2007 credit crunch, the shares took 65.8 months to climb back to their July 2007 high, a wait that ran through the whole 2008-2009 crisis.

KLA posted revenue of $13.6 billion for the four fiscal quarters ending June 30, 2026. Growth slowed to 11.7% during that period, down from 23.9% in the prior year. The company generates most of its sales through its Semiconductor Process Control segment. That division accounted for $10.9 billion of KLA’s $12.2 billion in total fiscal 2025 revenue.

The company recorded an operating margin of 41.7% over the latest twelve months, compared with 18.5% for the S&P 500. KLA’s twelve-month margin was below today’s 41.7% at 37 of the 40 quarter ends since fiscal 2017. The business also carries little debt. Total debt equals 2.9% of its market value, compared with 19.7% for the S&P 500.

During the July 28, 2026 call, management said KLA was “still dealing with some headwinds as related to memory pricing.” Memory is expected to make up about 27% of Semiconductor Process Control systems revenue from chip customers in the September quarter, management said.

Recent macroeconomic data, including hotter-than-expected inflation metrics, has pushed Treasury yields higher and rekindled investor concerns regarding sustained interest rate pressure. This macroeconomic environment has triggered a tactical rotation out of high-beta technology names into defensive sectors. Within the semiconductor space, market sentiment has turned increasingly cautious over the short-term durability of artificial intelligence infrastructure capital expenditures. As institutional investors scrutinize the capital intensity and return timelines for next-generation data centers, wafer fabrication equipment providers have borne the brunt of profit-taking.

Company-specific factors have amplified intraday volatility for KLA. Following an extended rally driven by robust demand for advanced process control and inspection tools, the stock traded at elevated valuation multiples compared to historical averages. This premium valuation made the equity particularly vulnerable to multiple compression during broad market pullbacks. Furthermore, recent capital flow data indicates notable net outflows from semiconductor-focused exchange-traded funds, alongside reported insider selling over recent months. With the company set to report its upcoming quarterly financial results later this month, short-term traders and institutional funds appear to be de-risking positions ahead of earnings to lock in prior gains.

Despite short-term trading pressure, KLA retains strong structural tailwinds tied to the long-term secular expansion of semiconductor complexity. As chip manufacturers scale leading-edge logic, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced packaging architectures, requirement intensity for process control and yield management continues to rise. The company maintains a substantial order backlog, providing clear revenue visibility across the coming fiscal quarters.

sum: A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after worries weighed on memory chipmakers and sparked selling pressure across the broader semiconductor sector, following news of domestic Chinese technological advancements and looming labor strikes in Taiwan.

As detailed by TipRanks, Chinese chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) announced significant progress on a next-generation 4F² DRAM server-memory design due by late 2026, launching denser DDR5 enterprise server modules that directly rival architectures currently being developed by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

However, the financial research firm added that CXMT has yet to prove it can manufacture the chips in commercial volumes. Amplifying the negative sentiment, Reuters, via Investing.com, reported that escalating labor tension in Taiwan added direct pressure on Micron, as 1,994 Taoyuan union members—representing 99% of ballots cast—voted to authorize a strike seeking a permanent 15% profit-sharing bonus. Investing.com noted that these Taiwan sites house 15,000 workers and anchor Micron's critical DRAM and high-bandwidth memory output, though no strike date has been set.

Consequently, shares of major memory manufacturers, including Micron, SanDisk, and SK Hynix, pulled back in early trade as these regional supply chain threats rattled investors.
